title: What is SPARC
text:
Cities in developing countries often lack current, reliable, and accessible geospatial data. Existing information is frequently fragmented across analogue or disconnected systems, costly to acquire and analyze, and difficult to reuse because of inconsistent licensing and limited technical capacity. As a result, World Bank Group teams, governments, and private investors may rely on outdated or low-resolution evidence when deciding where to invest in infrastructure, services, resilience, and urban development—slowing project preparation, duplicating costs, and increasing the risk of poorly targeted investments.
The Smart Parcel Atlas for Resilient Cities (SPARC) program addresses this gap by creating a shared, scalable platform for urban geospatial intelligence. The SPARC Toolkit on GeoInsight will combine quality-assured satellite imagery, global and city-specific datasets, standardized analytics, AI-enabled tools, and practical guidance in an interface accessible to non-specialists. There are three tiers of the SPARC program: 1. Tier 1 — Global urban data and analytics 2. Tier 2 — City-specific geospatial intelligence 3. Tier 3 — Operational uptake and client integration


Provides standardized, quality-assured geospatial data and automated statistics for approximately 10,000 cities worldwide. Includes city extent, built-up area, buildings, population, roads, administrative boundaries, and hazard data. Supports early operational scoping and serves as a “conversation starter” for country and city engagements. Made available through the SPARC Toolkit on GeoInsights for internal and external users.



Delivers higher-resolution, on-demand analytics for up to 100 priority cities. Supports investment option assessment and site prioritization through six initial services: buildings and parcels; urban public infrastructure; extreme heat exposure; multi-hazard exposure; green infrastructure; and urban settlement forecasts. Produces data layers, maps, analytical findings, and investment recommendations tailored to operational needs. Uses standardized workflows, centralized procurement, and partnerships to reduce the cost of each city analysis.



Connects SPARC analytics directly to World Bank Group operations and client decision-making. Regional operational teams lead demand identification, client engagement, local validation, and incorporation of findings into projects and local systems. Training, technical guidance, communications materials, and user-friendly GeoInsights tools help non-geospatial specialists interpret and apply the data. Ensures that the global and city-level analytics translate into better-targeted public and private investments.
The program will provide consistent urban data for roughly 10,000 cities worldwide while delivering higher-resolution, on-demand analytics for up to 100 cities in areas such as buildings and parcels, infrastructure access, heat and hazard exposure, green infrastructure, and future urban growth.
By centralizing data procurement, analytical workflows, technical support, and access, SPARC will reduce duplication and costs while improving data reuse across the World Bank Group and its clients. This shared “global technical backbone,” paired with regionally led client engagement, is intended to accelerate project preparation, improve the targeting of public and private investment, and support more resilient, productive, and inclusive urban development.

title: SPARC Building Scan
text:
The SPARC building scan is designed to extract and attribute building footprints for an entire city following a multistep process. To begin, we extract building footprints in the follow order:

Download buildings from Overture maps

Evaluate completeness of the downloaded building footprints through comparison to other built area data:

World Settlement Footprint

GHSL

[POTENTIALLY] Alpha Earth embeddings

Identify areas for infill from #2; perform infill using additional data sources:

HOT OSM tasking

Purchase satellite imagery and run building extraction locally

Purchase extracted building footprints from commercial providers


This notebook will focus on #1 and #2, with #3 being addressed in subsequent steps depending on the solution.

from pathlib import Path
import sys

import geopandas as gpd
from rasterio.mask import mask
from shapely.geometry import mapping, shape

sys.path.append("../src")
from building_coverage_helper import *

# auto reload modules
%load_ext autoreload
%autoreload 2


# Open the local city extent
CITY_EXTENTS_PATH = r"C:\WBG\Work\Projects\SPARC\building_scan\testing\CIV_UCDB_cities.geojson"
CITY_NAME_FIELD = "GC_UCN_MAI_2025"  # Update to a valid column in your extents file.

city_extents = gpd.read_file(CITY_EXTENTS_PATH)
city_extents = city_extents.to_crs(4326)

# Define output folder and files
OUTPUT_ROOT = Path(r"C:\WBG\Work\Projects\SPARC\building_scan\testing\output")
cities_folder = OUTPUT_ROOT / "cities"

for out_dir in [OUTPUT_ROOT, cities_folder]:
    Path(out_dir).mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)


for idx, row in city_extents.iterrows():
    city_name = row[CITY_NAME_FIELD]
    out_folder = cities_folder / city_name
    city_processor = SPARC_city(city_name, row, out_folder, city_extents.crs)
    city_processor.download_overture()
    city_processor.download_wsf()
    city_processor.compare_overture_wsf()
    break

title: SPARC Building Scan
text:
Welcome to the SPARC Building Scan project. This document provides an introduction to the project and guides you through the initial steps of using the analysis tools provided.
Tier 2 of the SPARC program focuses on tailored analytical products for individual cities. The Building Scan product is designed to provide detailed insights into the building stock of a city, including information on building types, heights, footprints, and other relevant attributes. This enables city planners, policymakers, and investors to make informed decisions regarding urban development, infrastructure planning, and risk assessment.


The Building Scan product generates several key outputs that provide comprehensive insights into the urban building landscape:

Building Footprints: Detailed mapping of the spatial extent of each building within the city.
Building Heights: Information on the vertical dimension of buildings, which is crucial for urban planning and risk assessment.
Building Age: Information on the age of buildings, which can be important for understanding the historical development of the city and for assessing the need for maintenance or retrofitting.
